claim: The Fulani ethnic group has relatively better protection from Plasmodium falciparum malaria, as reflected by fewer symptomatic cases of malaria, lower infection rates, and lower parasite densities compared to sympatric ethnic groups.
source: The Fulani ethnic group has relatively better protection from Plasmodium falciparum malaria, as reflected by fewer symptomatic cases of malaria, lower infection rates, and lower parasite densities compared to sympatric ethnic groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Targeted SNP analyses of candidate genes involved in the immune response to malaria have not been able to account for the observed difference in the Fulani susceptibility to P.falciparum.
source: targeted SNP analyses of other candidate genes involved in the immune response to malaria have not been able to account for the observed difference in the Fulani susceptibility to P.falciparum.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Arama et al., 2015a).

claim: Over 1000 genes were significantly differentially expressed in the monocyte fraction of the Fulani upon P.falciparum infection.
source: a strong transcriptional response was only detected in the monocyte fraction of the Fulani, where over 1000 genes were significantly differentially expressed upon P.falciparum infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Populations of Fulani living sympatrically with other ethnic groups from Mali to as far east as Sudan have consistently been reported to have fewer symptomatic cases of malaria, lower P.falciparum infection rates, and lower P.falciparum density in infected individuals.
source: Since the first report of the different response of Fulani to P.falciparum in 1996 (Modiano et al., 1996), populations of Fulani living sympatrically with other ethnic groups from Mali to as far east as Sudan, have consistently been reported to have fewer symptomatic cases of malaria, lower P.falciparum infection rates, and lower P.falciparum density in infected individuals (Arama et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Modiano et al., 1996; Arama et al., 2015a).

claim: Malaria has been a major selective force on the human genome in endemic areas.
source: Malaria has been a major selective force on the human genome in endemic areas
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citation.

claim: Enzymatic G6PD deficiency and abnormal hemoglobins such as HbS confer reduced susceptibility to malaria.
source: a number of factors conferring reduced susceptibility to malaria have been described, such as enzymatic G6PD deficiency, or abnormal hemoglobins - the most well know of which, HbS, confers sickle cell disease (Allison, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Allison, 2009) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Fulani are more responsive to P.falciparum antigens, with higher levels of P.falciparum specific IgG1-3, IgE and IgM antibodies.
source: Fulani are more responsive to P.falciparum antigens, with higher levels of P.falciparum specific IgG1-3, IgE and IgM antibodies (Modiano et al., 1996; Arama et al., 2015a; Arama et al., 2015b; Bolad et al., 2005; Vafa et al., 2009; Boström et al., 2012; Cherif et al., 2012; Maiga et al., 2014; Cherif et al., 2015; Cherif et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Fulani have a higher ratio of pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Fulani have a higher ratio of pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory cytokines (Boström et al., 2012; McCall et al., 2010; Arama et al., 2011; Farouk et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fulani have more activated memory B-cells.
source: Fulani have a different proportion of specific immune cells, including more activated memory B-cells (Portugal et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Portugal et al., 2012).

claim: Fulani have fewer circulating regulatory T-cells.
source: fewer circulating regulatory T-cells (McCall et al., 2010; Torcia et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fulani have increased activation of dendritic cells correlating with their lower frequency in circulating blood.
source: increased activation of dendritic cells correlating with their lower frequency in circulating blood (Arama et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Arama et al., 2011).

claim: The Fulani population had a significantly lower rate of P.falciparum infection compared to the Mossi.
source: The baseline characteristics presented in Figure 1a show that the Fulani population had a significantly lower rate of P.falciparum infection (Figure 1b)
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1b showing infection rates.

claim: The Fulani had significantly higher levels of P.falciparum specific antibodies (IgG) compared to the Mossi.
source: significantly higher levels of P.falciparum specific antibodies (IgG) (Figure 1c), consistent with previous reports (Boström et al., 2012; Arama et al., 2011; Perdijk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1c and citations to previous research.

claim: RNA-sequencing analysis of monocytes from uninfected Fulani compared to uninfected Mossi identified 17 significantly differentially expressed genes.
source: RNA-sequencing analysis of monocytes from uninfected Fulani (n = 7) compared to uninfected Mossi (n = 4) identified 17 significantly differentially expressed (DE) genes (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 2a.

claim: P2RX7 was the most significantly differentially expressed gene in monocytes from uninfected Fulani compared to uninfected Mossi.
source: The most significantly DE gene was P2RX 7 (Figure 2c), encoding P2X purinoceptor 7, a purinergic receptor for ATP that acts as a ligand-gated ion channel (Wiley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data in Figure 2c and citation to previous research.

claim: P2X purinoceptor 7 is a purinergic receptor for ATP that acts as a ligand-gated ion channel.
source: encoding P2X purinoceptor 7, a purinergic receptor for ATP that acts as a ligand-gated ion channel (Wiley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Wiley et al., 2011) and represents established knowledge.

claim: P2RX7 is highly expressed in immune cells, particularly monocytes.
source: P2RX7 is highly expressed in immune cells, particularly monocytes
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about P2RX7 expression patterns.

claim: Activation of P2RX7 drives the formation of the inflammasome and subsequent secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18.
source: its activation drives the formation of the inflammasome and subsequent secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 (Sharma and Kanneganti, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Sharma and Kanneganti, 2016).

claim: DNA methylation analysis of monocytes from the Mossi and the Fulani revealed only a few sites that were significantly differentially methylated.
source: DNA methylation analysis of monocytes from the Mossi and the Fulani revealed only a few sites that were significantly differentially methylated (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data presented in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The differentially methylated sites did not overlap with the differentially expressed genes identified by RNA-sequencing in monocytes from uninfected Fulani and Mossi.
source: These sites did not overlap with the DE genes identified by RNA-sequencing.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of RNA-sequencing and DNA methylation data.

claim: No differentially expressed genes were identified in the CD14– cells from uninfected Fulani and Mossi.
source: No DE genes were identified in the CD14– cells from uninfected Fulani and Mossi.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Infected Fulani monocytes had 1239 differentially expressed genes, most of which were downregulated (1095/1239).
source: infected Fulani had 1239 DE genes, most of which were downregulated (1095/1239) (Figure 2d and f, Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 2d and f, and Supplementary file 2B.

claim: Infected Mossi monocytes had only three differentially expressed genes.
source: in comparison, infected Mossi had only three DE genes (Figure 2e and f, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 2e and f, and Supplementary file 2C.

claim: The CD14– fraction from the same individuals did not display differences in gene expression upon P.falciparum infection.
source: The CD14– fraction from the same individuals did not display differences in gene expression (Figure 2g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 2g and h.

claim: The most significantly differentially expressed genes in monocytes of infected Fulani are involved in immune response, metabolism, cell cycle, chromatin and transcription regulation, RNA metabolism, translation, and ribosomal biogenesis.
source: The most significantly DE genes in monocytes of infected Fulani are involved in a variety of processes, including immune response, metabolism, cell cycle, chromatin and transcription regulation, RNA metabolism, translation, and ribosomal biogenesis (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by classification of differentially expressed genes shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Only a few genes were significantly differentially expressed between infected Fulani and infected Mossi monocytes.
source: Only a few genes were significantly differentially expressed between the two infected populations, suggesting that the majority of significantly DE genes in Fulani also experienced less significant changes in expression in Mossi. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data comparison presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2D.

claim: Fulani monocytes have a stronger transcriptional response to P.falciparum infection than Mossi monocytes.
source: This indicates that Fulani monocytes have a stronger transcriptional response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-sequencing data showing more differentially expressed genes in Fulani.

claim: The levels of pro-inflammatory IFN-γ were higher in blood plasma from uninfected Fulani than uninfected Mossi.
source: in agreement with this the levels of the pro-inflammatory IFN-γ were higher, and the levels of the anti-inflammatory TGF-β were lower, in blood plasma from uninfected Fulani than uninfected Mossi in our study (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3e and f.

claim: The levels of anti-inflammatory TGF-β were lower in blood plasma from uninfected Fulani than uninfected Mossi.
source: in agreement with this the levels of the pro-inflammatory IFN-γ were higher, and the levels of the anti-inflammatory TGF-β were lower, in blood plasma from uninfected Fulani than uninfected Mossi in our study (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3e and f.

claim: In individuals infected with P.falciparum, the levels of pro-inflammatory IFNγ and IL-6 were increased in the Mossi but reduced in the Fulani.
source: However, in individuals that were infected with P.falciparum, the levels of pro-inflammatory IFNγ and IL-6 were increased in the Mossi but reduced in the Fulani (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3f.

claim: Monocytes of uninfected Fulani are more immune reactive, driving different dynamics of response upon P.falciparum infection.
source: Collectively, these results indicate monocytes of uninfected Fulani are more immune reactive, driving different dynamics of response upon P.falciparum infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined transcriptional and cytokine data.

claim: Many of the differentially expressed genes in monocytes from infected Fulani are involved in the function of the inflammasome.
source: Many of the DE genes in monocytes from infected Fulani are involved in the function of the inflammasome (Supplementary file 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene classification data in Supplementary file 2E.

claim: The inflammasome is a cytoplasmic complex responsible for processing and activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18, and causing an inflammatory form of cell death - pyroptosis - via processing and activation of gasdermin D.
source: The inflammasome is a cytoplasmic complex responsible for processing and activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18, and causing an inflammatory form of cell death - pyroptosis - via processing and activation of gasdermin D (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Guo et al., 2015) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Monocytes from infected Fulani had significantly reduced expression of inflammasome pathway components including GSDMD, NLRP12, and NLRC5.
source: Monocytes from infected Fulani had significantly reduced expression of inflammasome pathway components (for example the gene encoding gasdermin D, GSDMD, and inflammasome complex scaffold proteins, NLRP12 [Ataide et al., 2014] and NLRC5 [Davis et al., 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: IL-1β was only detected in infected Fulani blood plasma.
source: IL-1β was only detected in infected Fulani
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3g.

claim: IL-18 was detected at higher levels in infected than uninfected Fulani blood plasma, whereas the levels in the Mossi did not change.
source: IL-18 was detected at higher levels in infected than uninfected Fulani, whereas the levels in the Mossi did not change (Figure 3g).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3g.

claim: The inflammasome was significantly more activated in infected Fulani than in the Mossi.
source: This indicates that the inflammasome was significantly more activated in infected Fulani than in the Mossi.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the IL-1β and IL-18 data.

claim: IL-1Ra and IL-18BPa showed higher levels in infected Fulani compared to uninfected Fulani.
source: These showed similar results, with higher levels in infected Fulani (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; IL-1Ra **p=0.0048, and IL-18BPa *p=0.0149, in infected compared to uninfected Fulani).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Fulani respond with a more active inflammasome, which results in feedback inhibition of the expression of inflammasome pathway components.
source: Our results suggest that the Fulani respond with a more active inflammasome, which results in feedback inhibition of the expression of inflammasome pathway components.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on inflammasome activation and gene expression.

claim: Transcription factor binding sites at the most significantly differentially expressed genes showed enrichment for ETS family transcription factors.
source: Analysis of transcription factor binding sites at the most significantly DE genes showed enrichment for ETS family transcription factors, which are downstream regulators of the MAPK and PI3K signalling pathways (Yordy and Muise-Helmericks, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: ETS family transcription factors are downstream regulators of the MAPK and PI3K signalling pathways.
source: which are downstream regulators of the MAPK and PI3K signalling pathways (Yordy and Muise-Helmericks, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Yordy and Muise-Helmericks, 2000) and represents established knowledge.

claim: A number of MAPK and PI3K pathway components were differentially expressed in monocytes from infected Fulani.
source: A number of MAPK and PI3K pathway components were differentially expressed, as was the ETS family transcription factor ERG.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Significantly differentially expressed genes were enriched in transcription factor binding sites for NF-κB and NRF2.
source: Significantly DE genes were also enriched in transcription factor binding sites for NF-κB and NRF2, signalling pathways that are directly regulated in activation of innate immune response pathways in monocytes (Dev et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis and citations to previous research.

claim: NF-κB and NRF2 signalling pathways are directly regulated in activation of innate immune response pathways in monocytes.
source: signalling pathways that are directly regulated in activation of innate immune response pathways in monocytes (Dev et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Genes involved in inducing different chromatin states and RNA metabolism were differentially expressed in monocytes from infected Fulani.
source: In addition to genes directly associated with innate immune response, genes involved in inducing different chromatin states and RNA metabolism were differentially expressed in monocytes from infected Fulani (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 4a.

claim: Monocytes from the Fulani have a capacity to remodel the chromatin landscape, which could result in a different or stronger transcriptional responses.
source: This suggests that monocytes from the Fulani have a capacity to remodel the chromatin landscape, which could result in a different or stronger transcriptional responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential expression of chromatin remodeling genes.

claim: PRDM5 was upregulated in monocytes of infected Fulani.
source: For example PRDM5, which is expressed in heamatapoietic stem cells where it is predicted to regulate chromatin organisation via association with architectural proteins CTCF, Cohesin, and TFIIIC (Riddell et al., 2014; Galli et al., 2013), was upregulated in monocytes of infected Fulani.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: PRDM5 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells where it is predicted to regulate chromatin organisation via association with architectural proteins CTCF, Cohesin, and TFIIIC.
source: which is expressed in heamatapoietic stem cells where it is predicted to regulate chromatin organisation via association with architectural proteins CTCF, Cohesin, and TFIIIC (Riddell et al., 2014; Galli et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Riddell et al., 2014; Galli et al., 2013).

claim: Components of the SWI/SNF complexes were differentially expressed in monocytes of infected Fulani.
source: Several chromatin remodelling components and histone modifying enzymes related to a more open chromatin state were differentially expressed; in particular components of the the SWI/SNF complexes, which are important for transcription of many immune genes and the phase shift to the adaptation phase in B-cells and T-cells (Foster et al., 2007; Schultze, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: SWI/SNF complexes are important for transcription of many immune genes and the phase shift to the adaptation phase in B-cells and T-cells.
source: which are important for transcription of many immune genes and the phase shift to the adaptation phase in B-cells and T-cells (Foster et al., 2007; Schultze, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Components of histone methyl transferase complexes SET1 and MLL complexes were differentially expressed in monocytes of infected Fulani.
source: and components of histone methyl transferase complexes SET1 and MLL complexes, both H3K4-me3 methyl transferases important in haematopoiesis (Yang and Ernst, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and citation to previous research.

claim: SET1 and MLL complexes are H3K4-me3 methyl transferases important in haematopoiesis.
source: both H3K4-me3 methyl transferases important in haematopoiesis (Yang and Ernst, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Yang and Ernst, 2017) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes responsible for inducing a silent chromatin state, such as SUV39H1, SUV420H1 and HDACs, were differentially expressed in monocytes of infected Fulani.
source: Genes encoding enzymes responsible for inducing a silent state, such as SUV39H1, SUV420H1 and HDACs, were also differentially expressed, indicating that the chromatin response to P.falciparum is complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: The chromatin response to P.falciparum in Fulani monocytes is complex.
source: indicating that the chromatin response to P.falciparum is complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential expression of both activating and repressing chromatin factors.

claim: Genes that are upregulated in response to P.falciparum infection in Mossi are already expressed at higher levels in uninfected Fulani.
source: Similar to the immune genes above, genes that are upregulated in response to P.falciparum infection in Mossi, are already expressed at higher levels in uninfected Fulani.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The observed differences in expression in monocytes of the Fulani was not caused by DNA-methylation.
source: The observed differences in expression in monocytes of the Fulani was not caused by DNA-methylation; the DNA methylation was very stable, with few differences between all analysed sample groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The few genes differentially methylated in monocytes from infected and uninfected Fulani did not correspond to the differentially expressed genes.
source: The few genes differentially methylated in monocytes from infected and uninfected Fulani did not correspond to the DE genes (Figure 4d, Supplementary files 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of DNA methylation and RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in monocytes of infected Fulani cluster in chromosomal regions.
source: Further analysis of DE genes in monocytes of infected Fulani, examining their chromosomal position, showed that they cluster in regions (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromosomal position analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The chromosomal regions containing clusters of differentially expressed genes displayed few differences in DNA methylation.
source: These regions displayed few differences in DNA methylation (Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation data presented in Figure 4g.

claim: A changed chromatin landscape underlies the altered gene expression pattern in Fulani monocytes.
source: This suggests that a changed chromatin landscape underlies the altered gene expression pattern.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on gene expression, DNA methylation, and chromosomal clustering.

claim: The higher levels of transcription of immune response genes in uninfected Fulani may drive a more immediate response following P.falciparum infection, and thus a more rapid and evident return to homeostatic levels of transcription.
source: First, the higher levels of transcription of immune response genes in uninfected Fulani may drive a more immediate response following P.falciparum infection, and thus a more rapid and evident return to homeostatic levels of transcription
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed data.

claim: An acute hyper-active response following P.falciparum infection may result in a subsequent hypo-active state in Fulani monocytes.
source: Second, an acute hyper-active response following P.falciparum infection may result in an subsequent hypo-active state.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed data.

claim: Genes involved in pathways which are rapidly activated under inflammatory conditions are significantly downregulated in infected Fulani, for example genes encoding aerobic glycolytic metabolism proteins (GAA and GAPDH).
source: This is supported by our results showing that genes involved in pathways which are rapidly activated under inflammatory conditions are significantly downregulated in infected Fulani, for example genes encoding aerobic glycolytic metabolism proteins (GAA and GAPDH; Figure 3—source data 1) (Lachmandas et al., 2016; McCall et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of the inflammasome occurs in two stages: first, a 'priming' signal activates expression of both inflammasome components and its target proteins; then, a second 'activation' signal promotes assembly of inflammasome components into an active complex that processes target proteins into their biologically active forms.
source: Activation of the inflammasome occurs in two stages: first, a 'priming' signal activates expression of both inflammasome components and its target proteins; then, a second 'activation' signal promotes assembly of inflammasome components into an active complex that processes target proteins into their biologically active forms (He et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (He et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Uninfected Fulani have higher baseline levels of expression of inflammasome pathway components, resulting in stronger inflammasome activation following P.falciparum infection.
source: Collectively, this suggests that the Fulani have higher baseline levels of expression of inflammasome pathway components, resulting in stronger inflammasome activation following P.falciparum infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on P2RX7 expression, inflammasome component expression, and cytokine levels.

claim: P.falciparum infection can drive inflammasome activation in human patients.
source: The available evidence indicates P.falciparum infection can drive inflammasome activation in human patients
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mice, hemozoin or symptomatic Plasmodium infection trigger inflammasome formation in erythrocytes and monocytes, respectively.
source: In mice, hemozoin or symptomatic Plasmodium infection trigger inflammasome formation in erythrocytes and monocytes, respectively (Ataide et al., 2014; Kalantari et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Monocytes from P.vivax malaria patients contain inflammasome components.
source: monocytes from P.vivax malaria patients contain inflammasome components (Ataide et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Ataide et al., 2014).

claim: P.falciparum and P.vivax DNA containing immunocomplexes induce inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation in human monocytes in culture.
source: P.falciparum and P.vivax DNA containing immunocomplexes induce inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation in human monocytes in culture (Hirako et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Hirako et al., 2015).

claim: Primed human monocyte-derived macrophages, incubated with antibody-opsonized P.falciparum infected erythrocytes, activate the inflammasome and secrete IL-1β.
source: and primed human monocyte-derived macrophages, incubated with antibody-opsonized P.falciparum infected erythrocytes, activate the inflammasome and secrete IL-1β (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: Activation of the inflammasome may be protective and involved in a more effective immune response in malaria.
source: Our results showing higher levels of inflammasome activation in P.falciparum infected Fulani support these findings, and further, suggest that activation of the inflammasome may be protective and involved in a more effective immune response in malaria.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data and previous research.

claim: In regions of hyperendemic malaria, individuals commonly experience multiple P.falciparum infections in a transmission season.
source: In regions of hyperendemic malaria, such as where the Fulani and the Mossi included in this study reside, individuals commonly experience multiple P.falciparum infections in a transmission season.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about malaria transmission in hyperendemic regions.

claim: Monocytes and other cells of the innate immune system have been reported to develop 'memory', enabling more efficient response to secondary infections.
source: In the case of other infections, monocytes and other cells of the innate immune system have been reported to develop 'memory', enabling more efficient response to secondary infections (Netea et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Netea et al., 2016).

claim: Trained immunity is typified by increased expression of different gene modules, upregulated proinflammatory cytokine response, and a shift toward aerobic glycolysis.
source: In contrast to innate immune tolerance, this response is typified by increased expression of different gene modules, upregulated proinflammatory cytokine response (Saeed et al., 2014), and a shift toward aerobic glycolysis (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trained immunity is based on epigenetic reprogramming of the innate immune cells.
source: This 'trained immunity' is based on epigenetic reprogramming of the innate immune cells (Netea et al., 2016; Glass and Natoli, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The transcriptional response in monocytes from infected Fulani is a result of an altered chromatin landscape caused by differential expression of chromatin remodelling and histone modification genes upon infection.
source: Instead, our results lead us to propose that the transcriptional response in monocytes from infected Fulani is a result of an altered chromatin landscape caused by differential expression of chromatin remodelling and histone modification genes upon infection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on gene expression and DNA methylation.

claim: Changes in chromatin structures and nuclear architecture occur both during differentiation and activation of immune cells.
source: Changes in chromatin structures and nuclear architecture, which depend on epigenetic changes as well as on density and spacing of nucleosomes, occur both during differentiation and activation of immune cells (Schultze, 2017; Netea et al., 2016; Glass and Natoli, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: The chromatin alterations predicted in Fulani are complex, involving both activators and repressors of chromatin states.
source: The chromatin alterations predicted in Fulani are complex, since differentially expressed genes are classified both as activators and repressors; for example, histone modifying enzymes such as SUV39H1 and SUV420H1, which are responsible for establishing heterochromatin were downregulated, as were those involved in establishing euchromain and activate promoters, such as SET1 and SWI/SNF.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-sequencing data showing differential expression of both activating and repressing chromatin factors.

claim: Non-coding RNAs contribute to the induction of chromatin states.
source: In addition, non-coding RNAs contribute to the induction of chromatin states (Rutenberg-Schoenberg et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Rutenberg-Schoenberg et al., 2016) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The few differentially expressed genes upregulated in the infected Fulani (144/1239) were enriched in non-coding RNA genes.
source: and the few DE genes upregulated in the infected Fulani (144/1239) were enriched in non-coding RNA genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: P.falciparum infections induce alteration in the chromatin landscape of monocytes.
source: Our conclusion that P.falciparum infections induce alteration in the chromatin landscape of monocytes is further supported by the observation that DE genes in Fulani monocytes often cluster in regions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the chromosomal clustering of differentially expressed genes.

claim: The chromosomal region 8q24.3 contains the c-Myc gene, GSDMD encoding inflammasome substrate gasdermin D, and a novel, uncharacterised locus of resistance to severe malaria.
source: Interestingly, one of these regions, 8q24.3 contains: the c-Myc gene; GSDMD, encoding inflammasome substrate gasdermin D (Liang and Liu, 2016); and a novel, uncharacterised locus of resistance to severe malaria (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromosomal position data and citations to previous research.

claim: Genome wide chromatin alterations occur as a result of P.falciparum infection in monocytes from Fulani, enabling a heightened transcriptional response.
source: Taken together we suggest that genome wide chromatin alterations occur as a result of P.falciparum infection in monocytes from Fulani, enabling a heightened transcriptional response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on gene expression, chromosomal clustering, and chromatin factor expression.

claim: Cells of the innate immune system, such as monocytes, macrophages and NK cells, exhibit memory alongside the more well studied memory of the adaptive immune system.
source: Cells of the innate immune system, such as monocytes, macrophages and NK cells, have been shown to exhibit a memory alongside the more well studied memory of the adaptive immune system.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about innate immune memory.

claim: Signalling pathways and transcription factors activated by the initial stimulus establish different histone modifications and nucleosome occupancy at specific sites.
source: Studies in model systems show that signalling pathways and transcription factors activated by the initial stimulus establish different histone modifications and nucleosome occupancy at specific sites (Foster et al., 2007; Netea et al., 2016; Glass and Natoli, 2016; Quintin et al., 2014; Hoeksema and de Winther, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trained immunity is characterised by an increased responsiveness of innate immune cells, typified by increased pro-inflammatory cytokine release and antimicrobial activity.
source: Trained immunity is characterised by an increased responsiveness of innate immune cells, typified by increased pro-inflammatory cytokine release and antimicrobial activity (Rizzetto et al., 2016; Netea and van der Meer, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trained immunity can persist months after an initial stimulus.
source: that can persit months after an initial stimulus (Netea et al., 2016; Quintin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Trained immunity correlates with epigenetic reprogramming at certain sites, with higher levels of H3K4me1/2 and H3K27Ac at specific gene promoters and enhancers.
source: Trained immunity correlates with epigenetic reprogramming at certain sites; ChIP sequencing analysis of monocytes show higher levels of H3K4me1/2 and H3K27Ac at specific gene promoters and enhancers, many of which are involved in pro-inflammatory response, metabolism, and phagocytosis (Saeed et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2014; Novakovic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The response observed in Fulani monocytes resembles trained immunity.
source: Our results show a response that resembles trained immunity in the Fulani.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of the observed data with characteristics of trained immunity.

claim: Chromatin factors that are involved in H3K4-methylation were significantly differentially expressed in Fulani monocytes.
source: For example, chromatin factors that are involved in H3K4-methylation were significantly differentially expressed.
